read.sections.0.heading.source: A building people keep working on
read.sections.0.heading.back: A building people keep working on

read.sections.0.text.source:
A building can last for generations because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need regular renewal, so keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage last. It means understanding what matters about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture: building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer religious and urban history. But its present structure should not simply be described as unchanged since medieval times.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A building can last for several generations because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different kinds of care. Some materials need to be renewed regularly, so keeping a place does not always mean leaving every surface untouched. Conservation is care that helps valued heritage keep lasting. It means understanding what is important about a building, and how its material, use and meaning can continue.

The Great Mosque of Djenné stands in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO names the Old Towns of Djenné as an important example of earthen architecture: building with materials made from earth. The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907. That date matters. The building we see is connected with a longer history of religion and the town. But the building that stands now should not simply be described as unchanged since the Middle Ages.
read.sections.0.text.note: "conservation" is "konservasi", as Southeast Asia's TERMS. "earthen architecture" is "arsitektur tanah".

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A building can last a long time because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must be renewed often. So keeping a place does not always mean leaving it untouched. Conservation is care that helps a valued place last. It means knowing what matters about a building, and how to keep it going.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO calls Djenné's old towns a key example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. We should not say it is unchanged since long ago.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A building can last a long time because people keep working on it. Roofs, walls and surfaces need different care. Some materials must be renewed often. So keeping a place does not always mean not touching it. Conservation is care that helps a valuable place last. It means knowing what is important about a building, and how to keep it there.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is in Mali, in West Africa. UNESCO calls the old towns of Djenné a main example of earthen architecture. That means buildings made with earth. The mosque we see now was rebuilt in 1906 and 1907. The town's history is much older. We must not say the mosque has not changed since very long ago.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque mattered. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. It became important for the spread of Islam in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Waterways also linked the town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local building knowledge belonged to the same urban history. Islamic identity did not require copying one form of building used everywhere. People used regional materials and skills to make a place of worship suited to their setting.

Earth is a skilled building material here. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas describes sun-baked earth bricks coated with mud plaster. The wooden pieces that stick out from the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photographs in this lesson show parts of the outside in 2005. They record what was visible then; they do not show the building's condition today.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The town's wider setting explains why this mosque is important. Djenné grew as a market centre connected with the trans-Saharan gold trade, that is, the trade in gold across the Sahara Desert. This town became important for the spread of Islam in the 15th and 16th centuries. Waterways also connected this town with other trading places. Trade, religious learning and local knowledge about building belonged to the same history of the town. Islamic identity did not require people to copy one form of building used everywhere. People used materials and skills from their region to make a place of worship that suited their surroundings.

Here, earth is a building material that needs skill. UNESCO's Urban Heritage Atlas (Urban Heritage Atlas) describes earth bricks dried in the sun and coated with mud plaster. The pieces of wood that stick out of the walls, and the shaped surfaces, give the mosque a distinctive look. The photos in this lesson show parts of its outside in 2005. The photos record what was visible at that time; they do not show the building's condition in the present.

People here used local materials and skills. They made a mosque that suits its place.

Earth is a skilled building material here. The bricks are made of earth and dried in the sun. Builders cover them with mud plaster. Wooden pieces stick out from the walls. The photos in this lesson were taken in 2005. They show how the mosque looked then, not how it looks today.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné
read.sections.2.heading.back: Care, knowledge and the people of Djenné

read.sections.2.text.source:
Looking after earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, the skilled builders, and how building skills are passed on. It also names the yearly plastering of the mosque as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the physical building. Intangible heritage is the knowledge, organisation and shared practices around it. People take part in the life of the place through work as well as worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to recover or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that yearly surface care and specialist repairs to the structure are different kinds of work. It should not be read as a current report of an emergency still going on.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to consider those lives. Treating a place only as attractive scenery can leave out the people whose knowledge keeps it going. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how they are looked after. It also asks how decisions involve the communities who use them.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Caring for earthen buildings depends on knowledge and cooperation. The atlas describes Djenné's masons, that is, the skilled builders, and how building skills are passed down. The atlas also names the plastering of the mosque every year as a practice that connects two kinds of heritage. Tangible cultural heritage is the physical building. Intangible cultural heritage is the knowledge, the organisation of work and the shared practices around it. People take part in the life of that place through work, as well as through worship.

Regular care does not prevent every problem. A UNESCO report from December 2009 describes extra restoration and strengthening work involving traditional masons. Restoration is work to recover or make clearer an earlier form or condition. This dated report shows that care of the surface every year and specialist repairs to the building's structure are two different kinds of work. The report must not be read as the latest report about an emergency that is still going on.

Djenné is also a town where people live, trade and learn, and want comfortable homes and public services. Conservation needs to pay attention to their lives. Treating a place only as beautiful scenery can forget the people whose knowledge keeps that place there. A careful account asks which features carry historical and cultural meaning, and how those features are cared for. It also asks how decisions involve the communities that use them.
read.sections.2.text.note: "tangible / intangible heritage" are "warisan budaya benda / takbenda", the official Indonesian terms (Warisan Budaya Takbenda Indonesia). "restoration" is "pemugaran", as Southeast Asia's TERMS for buildings. "masons" is "tukang bangunan".

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Caring for earth buildings takes skill and teamwork. Djenné's masons are skilled builders. They pass their skills on to others. Every year, people put new plaster on the mosque. This links two kinds of heritage. Tangible heritage is the building itself. Intangible heritage is the knowledge and shared ways of doing things. People help the mosque through work as well as worship.

Yearly care cannot stop every problem. In December 2009, a UNESCO report told of extra repairs. Masons who use old skills did the work. Restoration is work to bring back an earlier form or condition. So the yearly plaster and big repairs are different jobs. That report is from 2009. It does not describe a problem today.

People also live, trade and learn in Djenné. They want good homes and services. Conservation must think about their lives too. A place is not just a pretty view. The people who keep it going matter. Good choices include the people who use the place.

People help the mosque through work, as well as through worship.

write.prompt.source: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail of each from the reading.
write.prompt.back: Explain why caring for the mosque needs both materials and people's knowledge. Use one detail about each from the reading.

write.example.source: The mosque is made of earth bricks and mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people put new plaster on the mosque every year. People's knowledge matters too. Djenné's masons know how to do this work, and they pass their skills on to others. The building lasts because of both its earth and the people who look after it.
write.example.back: The mosque is made of earth bricks and mud plaster. This material needs care again and again, so people put new plaster on the mosque every year. People's knowledge also matters. Djenné's masons know how to do this work, and they pass their skills on to other people. The building lasts because of its earth and also because of the people who care for it.

educatorNotes.0.source: Misconception to watch for: authentic heritage must never change, or building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the documented techniques and the continuing social life of Djenné.
educatorNotes.0.back: Misconception to watch for: that authentic heritage must never change at all, or that building with earth shows a lack of skill. Both hide the recorded techniques and the social life of Djenné that continues.

educatorNotes.4.source: Don't merge the present town and mosque with the older archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, or with the borders of a single medieval empire. The trade, Islam and waterway context comes from the UNESCO site record and the atlas.
